source_read: PDF, pp. 129-138 (all pages; Tables 1-6 checked on pages rendered at 110 dpi). Step 1 (blind extraction) not run this round, per the round brief.

design.note: Cross-sectional comparison of two groups measured once, with no pre-use measure; the card's one-sentence statement of what the design can and cannot establish matches the paper.

key_findings.note: Checked against p. 132 (5-HIAA, 1st paragraph) and Table 4 on the rendered p. 133. Means, SDs, range, both F values and the editors' 32% and Welch interval (1.7 to 8.1) all recomputed and agree.

Checked p. 132 and Table 4 with its four footnotes: the section symbol marks MDMA women against control women and MDMA men carry no marker. Recomputed the editors' Welch figures: men 2.6 (-0.6 to 5.8), p about .10; women 8.6 (2.2 to 15.0), p about .012.
Checked p. 132, 3rd paragraph of the 5-HIAA subsection; r = -0.2, p = .33, and the three other use variables stated as non-significant without coefficients.
Checked p. 132 (2nd paragraph) and p. 135 (Discussion, 2nd paragraph). Recomputed Fisher z for the two correlations: 2.27, p about .023.
Checked p. 132, 4th paragraph: F(3, 50) = .89, p = .45, and the statement that comparable numbers were examined in each season.
Checked pp. 132-133 and Table 4. Recomputed the editors' Welch tests: overall p about .070, women p about .11. Table 4 prints control women's SD as 29.9 and a control range to 117.9.
Checked p. 133 (Prolactin, 1st and 2nd paragraphs) and Table 5.
Checked p. 134 (Pain Measures) and Table 6; F values, p values and the absence of group effects as stated.
Checked p. 134 (MPQ, BDHI and EPQ paragraphs); F values and the post hoc pattern as stated.

Checked Table 3 on the rendered p. 131: every count and percentage matches. Recomputed the editors' Fisher exact tests: cocaine .0002, hallucinogens <.001, benzodiazepines .004, sedative-hypnotics .006, amphetamines .021, cannabis .138. All agree.
Checked p. 135, Discussion 1st paragraph: both statements are there.
Checked p. 136, Discussion 6th and 7th paragraphs: the three alternatives are in the 6th, the response-bias argument in the 7th.

reporting_issues.note: Table 2, p. 131: 170 plus or minus .82 mg with range 0.5 to 4, footnoted as capsules or tablets; p. 135 refers to one tablet or capsule. The row cannot be read as printed.
Table 3, p. 131: 22 of 28 is 78.6%, and no whole number out of 28 gives 73%.
p. 135 Discussion against Table 1 and Table 3 (p. 131); the mismatch is as described, and no analysis adjusts for other drug use.
p. 134: printed F(1, 52) = 4.4, p = .004 for the alienation interaction. Recomputed: p = .041 for that F, so one of the two is misprinted.
pp. 132-133: Table 4 carries no marker on the overall HVA row although the text reports p = .01; the editors' unequal-variance recomputation (p about .070 overall, .11 in women) agrees.
p. 132: F(3, 50) printed. Recomputed: a 2 x 4 design with two covariates in 58 people leaves 48 error degrees of freedom.
p. 133, Table 5: 16 + 18 + 7 + 10 = 51 of 58, with no explanation.

pp. 134, 136: the Results give p values only (alienation p < .0001 and control p = .06 in women; harm-avoidance p = .02 and constraint p = .07 in men), and the Discussion then treats the control correlation as a finding.
pp. 132, 134: Methods name age and education as covariates for the personality analyses; the MPQ paragraph names age only.
p. 134 and Table 6: the text reports gender effects only, while Table 6 shows MDMA men below control men on endurance (9.9 vs 12.2) and tolerance (114 vs 157), with no group statistics.

instrument.note: ROBINS-E is the right instrument for a non-randomized study of an exposure (METHODS 5.3).

domains.note: High is right: the group difference in other drug use is large (cocaine 80% vs 29%, hallucinogens 87% vs 32%) and nothing is adjusted for it.
High is right: the MDMA group reached the study by telephoning an investigator about MDMA research, and some controls were referred by them.
The content (time since last use, abstinence verified only on arrival) belongs more naturally under measurement of the exposure, but the judgment is not affected.
Some concerns is driven by the prolactin measure (51 of 58); for the main outcome, CSF, the data are complete and this domain would be low.
Low for CSF is right (fixed diet, fixed time of day, bed rest, assays blind to group, coefficients of variation 2.3% and 4.7%); the card already says the self-report personality outcomes are weaker.

overall.note: High, and not less severe than the worst domain. The restriction in the reasoning (citable for lower lumbar CSF 5-HIAA in this group, not for damage, dose-response or cognition) matches what I read.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial is right. The title and summary state serotonin neurotoxicity while the Discussion concedes that CSF data alone cannot establish the nature of the alteration, and the matching described on p. 135 is contradicted by Tables 1 and 3.

missed: The paper's own explanation of the sex difference (p. 135) is that women were exposed more: they reported about 115 occasions against 85 for men and weighed less while reporting the same amount per occasion. This sits awkwardly beside the finding that 5-HIAA had no relation to the number of exposures (r = -0.2, p = .33) within the group, and the card does not bring the two together. It matters for any dose-response reading of this study.

The authors explain the normal prolactin response by possible recovery of serotonin axons to the hypothalamus in the months after exposure, citing monkey work, and note that participants had last used MDMA about 18 weeks earlier, some up to 2 years (p. 135). That argument is evidence the encyclopedia will need for reversibility and for the tolerance question (METHODS 8, section 5), and the card's interpretation-gap field does not record it.

Table 5 shows MDMA women with a higher post-tryptophan prolactin peak than control women (33.8 vs 30.3) and MDMA men higher than control men (14.8 vs 13.4): the neuroendocrine result is not merely non-significant but numerically in the opposite direction to a blunted response. Worth one line, because the 1988 report this study sets aside had claimed blunting.

The study tested nobody's memory or thinking, so it cannot be cited anywhere on the cognition claims; the card says so under cannot_establish, but the key findings would be easier to use if that were also stated in the replication/where-it-stands field, which currently discusses only CSF studies.
